book.title: I Will Teach You to Be Rich
book.author: Ramit Sethi

confidence_note: Thin sourcing: details come from a book review, Sethi's website (Next $100 principle, stylist example via a news piece) and a summary giving bucket percentages; none checked against the 2009 text. The old text's $1,500 coffee figure, rent 30-40 percent, car costs and compounding raise were dropped as unverified. The 25-33 percent cut is Sethi's own target for his own two categories, not a promised result. Overlaps 1606 on the buckets.
facts: Sethi is famously indifferent to cutting daily lattes and avoids tracking every penny; he focuses on the five to ten decisions that drive most results ('Big Wins'), including automating savings and negotiating salary.
Conscious spending plan: a budget looks backward, a plan lets you look forward; spend extravagantly on what you love, cut costs mercilessly on what you do not.

Four buckets: fixed costs, investments, savings, guilt-free spending; one summary: fixed costs about 50-60 percent of take-home, investments about 10 percent, savings 5-10 percent, guilt-free spending the remainder.

Next $100 principle (website): pick the top two discretionary expenses (his: eating out and going out), cut them 25-33 percent over six months, send the cash to investing and travel; big wins come from a couple of categories rather than trimming everything a little.
Once bills are paid and saving/investing automated, the remaining money is yours to spend; his example is a personal stylist because he enjoys dressing well.
scene_details: eating out and going out as his own two categories
a personal stylist as his own spending example
tension: A money book that does not ask you to give up the daily coffee but asks you to cut hard elsewhere.
opening_idea: Open on the latte surviving untouched and the stylist, then the short list of bigger things.

lessons.idea: Cut where costs are big and keep what you love.
lessons.anchor: Next $100: two biggest discretionary expenses; the latte left alone.
lessons.example: Someone gives up takeaway coffee but ignores a yearly gym fee for a gym they do not use.

reflect_final: Of everything you spend on without much thought, which one or two items are large enough to matter and which of them would you truly miss?

use_cases.situation: You are about to cancel a small treat to save money.
use_cases.move: List your two biggest optional costs first and cut the one you barely use.

use_cases.situation: A partner wants to cut small pleasant spending.
use_cases.move: Quote the rule to cut mercilessly on what you do not love and ask which two things you would miss.

use_cases.situation: A team trims many tiny costs.
use_cases.move: Look at the two biggest optional costs first.

pocket_idea: Keep the small pleasure; check your two biggest optional costs first.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Sethi is indifferent to the latte and cuts hard on the two biggest optional costs.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: No latte ban; 5-10 big decisions; Next $100 on two biggest discretionary expenses cut 25-33 percent; rest is yours.
